chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-1.title: Reduce the degree
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-1.body:
Since $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$ we have $\omega^n=\omega^{n-2}\omega^2=-\omega^{n-1}-\omega^{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$. Hence for $z=a_0+\dots+a_n\omega^n$ with $n\ge2$,
$$z=a_0+\dots+a_{n-3}\omega^{n-3}+(a_{n-2}-a_n)\omega^{n-2}+(a_{n-1}-a_n)\omega^{n-1},$$
which is again a combination of powers of $\omega$ with integer coefficients, now of degree at most $n-1$. Repeating, we reach degree at most $1$: $z=a+b\omega$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-2.title: Expand using $\omega^2=-1-\omega$
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-2.body:
$$(a_1+b_1\omega)(a_2+b_2\omega)=a_1a_2+(a_1b_2+a_2b_1)\omega+b_1b_2\omega^2=(a_1a_2-b_1b_2)+(a_1b_2+a_2b_1-b_1b_2)\omega.$$
Both coefficients are integers, so the product lies in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-3b.title: Use the conjugate
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-3b.body: Since $\omega^2=\bar\omega$ (as $\omega\bar\omega=|\omega|^2=1$ and $\omega^3=1$), we have $a+b\omega^2=\overline{a+b\omega}$. Therefore $(a+b\omega)(a+b\omega^2)=|a+b\omega|^2=N(a+b\omega)$ by part (a). $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-4.title: Modulus is multiplicative
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-4.body: By Problem 1-3a, $N(z)=|z|^2$ for every Eisenstein integer, and $z_1z_2\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$ (Problem 1-2). So $N(z_1z_2)=|z_1z_2|^2=|z_1|^2|z_2|^2=N(z_1)N(z_2)$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-6a.title: Multiply the inverses
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-6a.body: If $\alpha_1\beta_1=1$ and $\alpha_2\beta_2=1$ with $\beta_j\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$, then $(\alpha_1\alpha_2)(\beta_1\beta_2)=1$ and $\beta_1\beta_2\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$ (closure under products). $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-6b.title: Use the inverse
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-6b.body: Let $\beta\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$ with $\alpha\beta=1$. Then $\beta=1/\alpha$, so $z/\alpha=z\beta$, a product of two Eisenstein integers, hence an Eisenstein integer. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-6c.title: Multiplicativity
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-6c.body: With $\alpha\beta=1$, multiplicativity gives $N(\alpha)N(\beta)=N(1)=1$. Both norms are non-negative integers, so $N(\alpha)=1$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-7.title: Find all elements of norm 1
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-1-7.body:
*Each listed number is a unit:* $\omega^3=1$ gives inverses $\omega^2$ for $\omega$ and $\omega$ for $\omega^2$, and $\pm1$ are self-inverse (up to sign).

*Conversely*, a unit has norm $1$ (Problem 1-6c). Fix an integer $b$ and view $a^2-ab+b^2=\left(a-\frac b2\right)^2+\frac{3b^2}4$. If $b$ is even and nonzero, this is $\ge\frac{3b^2}4\ge3$. If $b$ is odd, the smallest integer values of $a$ give $a=\frac{b\pm1}2$ and the value $\frac{3b^2+1}4$, which is $1$ for $|b|=1$ and at least $7$ for $|b|\ge3$. So $N=1$ forces $b\in\{-1,0,1\}$; by symmetry in $a,b$ (as $N(a+b\omega)$ is symmetric) also $a\in\{-1,0,1\}$. Checking the nine pairs: $N=1$ exactly for $(a,b)\in\{(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1),(\mp1,\mp1)\}$, i.e. $\pm1$, $\pm\omega$, and $-1-\omega=\omega^2$, $1+\omega=-\omega^2$; the remaining pairs give $N=0$ or $3$. So the elements of norm $1$ are exactly $\pm1,\pm\omega,\pm\omega^2$, and they are the units. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-1b.title: Factor $\rho$
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-1b.body:
$\gamma\beta\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$, so $\rho=\alpha-\gamma\beta\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$. Since $\alpha=z\beta$, $\rho=(z-\gamma)\beta$, and norm (the squared modulus) is multiplicative:
$$N(\rho)=N(z-\gamma)N(\beta)\le\tfrac34N(\beta)<N(\beta).$$
So $\alpha=\gamma\beta+\rho$ with $0\le N(\rho)<N(\beta)$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-2.title: Minimal norm generator
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-2.body:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb Z[\omega]$ be an ideal. If $I=\{0\}$ it is generated by $0$. Otherwise choose $\beta\in I$, $\beta\ne0$, of minimal norm (norms are positive integers, so a minimum exists). The multiples of $\beta$ lie in $I$. Conversely, let $\alpha\in I$ and write $\alpha=\gamma\beta+\rho$ with $N(\rho)<N(\beta)$. Then $\rho=\alpha-\gamma\beta\in I$, and minimality of $N(\beta)$ forces $\rho=0$. So $\alpha=\gamma\beta$ and $I=(\beta)$.

For $\mathbb Z$ the same argument works with $|\cdot|$ in place of the norm and ordinary division with remainder. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-3.title: Division algorithm
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-3.body:
$N(2+\omega)=4-2+1=3$, and $\frac{13}{2+\omega}=\frac{13(2+\omega^2)}{(2+\omega)(2+\omega^2)}=\frac{13(2+\omega^2)}3=\frac{26}3+\frac{13}3\omega^2=\frac{13}3-\frac{13}3\omega$ (using $\omega^2=-1-\omega$). Rounding the coefficients gives $\gamma=4-4\omega$. Then
$$\rho=13-(4-4\omega)(2+\omega)=13-(8-4\omega-4\omega^2)=13-12=1,$$
with $N(\rho)=1<3$.

**Answer: $\gamma=4-4\omega$, $\rho=1$.** (The quotient and remainder are not unique here; any valid pair is correct.)

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-4.title: Find the pair, then prove uniqueness
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-2-4.body:
$N(3-2\omega)=9+6+4=19$ and $19=(3-2\omega)(3-2\omega^2)$ (norm formula), so $\gamma=3-2\omega^2$, $\rho=0$ works.

If $(\gamma',\rho')$ is another solution with $\gamma'\ne\gamma$, then $\rho'=19-\gamma'(3-2\omega)=(3-2\omega)(\gamma-\gamma')\ne0$, so $N(\rho')=N(3-2\omega)N(\gamma-\gamma')\ge N(3-2\omega)$ because $N(\gamma-\gamma')\ge1$ for a nonzero Eisenstein integer. This violates $N(\rho')<N(3-2\omega)$. Hence the pair is unique. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-1.title: Transfer divisibility
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-1.body:
Let $uv=1$. Suppose $\pi$ is an Eisenstein prime. Then $u\pi\ne0$ and $u\pi$ is not a unit (otherwise $\pi=v(u\pi)$ would be a unit). If $u\pi\mid\alpha\beta$ then $\pi\mid\alpha\beta$, so $\pi\mid\alpha$ or $\pi\mid\beta$, say $\alpha=\kappa\pi=(\kappa v)(u\pi)$, so $u\pi\mid\alpha$. Hence $u\pi$ is an Eisenstein prime.

Conversely if $u\pi$ is an Eisenstein prime, apply the same argument with the unit $v$ to $u\pi$ to get that $v(u\pi)=\pi$ is an Eisenstein prime. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-2.title: Euclidean division
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-2.body:
Let $p=N(z)$. Then $z
e0$ and $z$ is not a unit ($p>1$). Suppose $z\mid\alpha eta$ but $z
mid\alpha$ and $z
mid eta$. Divide: $\alpha=\gamma_1z+ho_1$, $ eta=\gamma_2z+ho_2$ with $0\le N(ho_j)<p$; since $z
mid\alpha, eta$, both remainders are nonzero, so $1\le N(ho_j)\le p-1$. Then $ho_1ho_2=(\alpha-\gamma_1z)( eta-\gamma_2z)\equiv\alpha eta\equiv0$ modulo $z$, i.e. $ho_1ho_2=\kappa z$, so $N(ho_1)N(ho_2)=N(\kappa)p$ is a multiple of the prime $p$. But $p
mid N(ho_1)$ and $p
mid N(ho_2)$ (both are between $1$ and $p-1$), so $p
mid N(ho_1)N(ho_2)$, a contradiction. $ lacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-3b.title: Irreducible implies prime
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-3b.body:
*$p$ is irreducible.* If $p=\mu
u$ with non-units $\mu,
u$, then $N(\mu)N(
u)=p^2$ with $N(\mu),N(
u)>1$, so $N(\mu)=p\equiv2\pmod3$, contradicting Problem 3-3a. Also $p$ is not a unit ($N(p)=p^2>1$).

*Irreducible implies prime.* Suppose $p\mid\alpha eta$ and $p
mid\alpha$. The ideal $J=\{x p+y\alpha:x,y\in\mathbb Z[\omega]\}$ is principal, $J=(\delta)$. Since $p\in J$, $\delta\mid p$, so (by irreducibility) $\delta$ is a unit or an associate of $p$. If $\delta$ were an associate of $p$, then $\alpha\in J$ would be divisible by $p$, contrary to assumption. So $\delta$ is a unit and $1\in J$: $1=xp+y\alpha$. Multiply by $ eta$: $ eta=xp eta+y\alpha eta$, and both terms are divisible by $p$. So $p\mid eta$. Hence $p$ is an Eisenstein prime. $ lacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-4.title: Explicit factorization
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-4.body: $(-1+\omega)(-1+\omega^2)=1-\omega-\omega^2+\omega^3=2-(\omega+\omega^2)=3$. Each factor has norm $N(-1+\omega)=1+1+1=3$, a rational prime, so both are Eisenstein primes by Problem 3-2 (the conjugate $-1+\omega^2$ has the same norm). Finally $-\omega^2(-1+\omega)=\omega^2-\omega^3=\omega^2-1=-1+\omega^2$, so they are associates. $3=\pi_1\pi_2$ is a product of two primes, so $3$ itself is not prime (it divides $\pi_1\pi_2$ but neither factor, since their norms $3<9$). $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-5.title: Pigeonhole, then factor
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-5.body:
**(b).** Since $3\mid p-1$ and $(\mathbb Z/p)^*$ is cyclic, there is $s$ of order $3$ modulo $p$, so $s^3\equiv1$, $s\not\equiv1$ and $s^2+s+1\equiv0\pmod p$.

Let $k=\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$. The $(k+1)^2>p$ pairs $(x,y)$ with $0\le x,y\le k$ give only $p$ residues $x-sy\bmod p$, so two distinct pairs satisfy $x_1-sy_1\equiv x_2-sy_2$. Put $a=x_1-x_2$, $b=y_2-y_1$: then $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, $|a|,|b|\le k<\sqrt p$, and $a\equiv-sb\pmod p$. Hence
$$a^2-ab+b^2\equiv s^2b^2+sb^2+b^2=b^2(s^2+s+1)\equiv0\pmod p.$$
Also $0<a^2-ab+b^2\le a^2+|ab|+b^2<3p$, so $a^2-ab+b^2\in\{p,2p\}$. But norms are $\equiv0,1\pmod3$ (Problem 3-3a) and $2p\equiv2$. Thus $a^2-ab+b^2=p$, proving (b).

**(a).** With $a,b$ from (b), $p=N(a+b\omega)=(a+b\omega)(a+b\omega^2)$ and both factors have norm $p$ (the second is the complex conjugate of the first). By Problem 3-2 both are Eisenstein primes. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-6a.title: Check the axioms
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-6a.body: $0\in I\cap\mathbb Z$. If $z_1,z_2\in I\cap\mathbb Z$ then $z_1+z_2\in I$ (ideal) and $\in\mathbb Z$. If $z\in I\cap\mathbb Z$ and $a\in\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Z[\omega]$, then $az\in I$ and $az\in\mathbb Z$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-6b.title: Use primality
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-6b.body: $ab\in I$ means $\pi\mid ab$, so $\pi\mid a$ or $\pi\mid b$, i.e. $a\in I$ or $b\in I$; both are integers. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-6c.title: Principal ideal of $\mathbb Z$
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-6c.body: By 3-6a and Problem 2-2, $I\cap\mathbb Z=n\mathbb Z$ for some $n\ge0$. The integer $N(\pi)=\pi\bar\pi$ is nonzero and lies in $I$, so $n\ne0$. If $n=1$ then $1\in I$ and $\pi$ would be a unit, so $n\ge2$. If $n=rs$ with $1<r,s<n$, then $rs\in I\cap\mathbb Z$, so by 3-6b $n\mid r$ or $n\mid s$, impossible for $0<r,s<n$. Hence $n=p$ is a rational prime and $p\in I$, i.e. $\pi\mid p$. It is unique since $p\mathbb Z=I\cap\mathbb Z$ determines $p$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-7.title: Classification
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-7.body:
*The three types are prime:* (ii) and (iii) by Problem 3-2 (norm a prime), (i) by Problems 3-3b and 3-1.

*Every prime is of one of the types.* Let $\pi$ be an Eisenstein prime with $\pi\mid p$ ($p$ a rational prime). Then $N(\pi)\mid N(p)=p^2$ and $N(\pi)\ne1$, so $N(\pi)\in\{p,p^2\}$.

- If $N(\pi)=p$: by Problem 3-3a, $p\not\equiv2\pmod3$, so $p=3$ (type ii) or $p\equiv1\pmod3$ (type iii).
- If $N(\pi)=p^2$: write $p=\pi\kappa$; then $N(\kappa)=1$, so $\kappa$ is a unit and $p$ is an associate of $\pi$, hence an Eisenstein prime (3-1). But $3$ is not prime (3-4) and a prime $p\equiv1\pmod3$ is not prime either: $p=(a+b\omega)(a+b\omega^2)$ with factors of norm $p<p^2$, which $p$ cannot divide. So $p\equiv2\pmod3$ (type i). $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-8a.title: Split $91=7\cdot13$
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-8a.body:
$N(2-\omega)=4+2+1=7$ and $N(4+\omega)=16-4+1=13$, so (Problem 3-2) $2-\omega,2-\omega^2$ (norm $7$) and $4+\omega,4+\omega^2$ (norm $13$) are Eisenstein primes, and $(2-\omega)(2-\omega^2)=7$, $(4+\omega)(4+\omega^2)=13$ by Problem 1-3b. Hence
$$91=(2-\omega)(2-\omega^2)(4+\omega)(4+\omega^2).$$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-8b.title: Factor out $5\omega^2$
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-3-8b.body:
$15\omega^2-25=\omega^2(15-25\omega)=5\omega^2(3-5\omega)$ (using $\omega^3=1$). Since $5\equiv2\pmod3$, $5$ is an Eisenstein prime (3-3b) and so is its associate $5\omega^2$ (3-1). Next $N(3-5\omega)=9+15+25=49=7^2$, and $(2-\omega)^2=4-4\omega+\omega^2=3-5\omega$ with $N(2-\omega)=7$, a prime, so $2-\omega$ is an Eisenstein prime. Therefore
$$15\omega^2-25=5\omega^2\,(2-\omega)(2-\omega).$$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-1.title: Eisenstein integers of norm 2023
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-1.body:
$a^2-ab+b^2=N(a+b\omega)$ and $2023=7\cdot17^2$. By the classification, an Eisenstein integer of norm $2023$ is a product of primes whose norms multiply to $2023$: the rational prime $17\equiv2\pmod3$ is itself an Eisenstein prime (norm $17^2$), and the rest must be a prime of norm $7$, i.e. an associate of $2-\omega$ or $2-\omega^2$ (where $7=(2-\omega)(2-\omega^2)$). So the elements of norm $2023$ are the $12$ numbers $u\cdot17(2-\omega)$ and $u\cdot17(2-\omega^2)$, $u$ a unit.

Listing them as $a+b\omega$ (using $\omega^2=-1-\omega$) and keeping those with $a,b>0$ gives
$$(a,b)\in\{(17,51),(34,51),(51,17),(51,34)\}$$
For example $17(2-\omega^2)=51+17\omega$, $-\omega^2\cdot17(2-\omega^2)=34+51\omega$, $-\omega^2\cdot17(2-\omega)=51+34\omega$ and $\omega\cdot17(2-\omega)=17+51\omega$; the other eight unit multiples have a non-positive coefficient.

**Answer: $(17,51),(34,51),(51,17),(51,34)$.** A direct search over $1\le a,b\le200$ confirms exactly these four pairs.

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-2a.title: Count prime factors by norm
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-2a.body:
Solutions $(a,b)$ correspond to Eisenstein integers $z=a+b\omega$ with $N(z)=n$.

*Necessity.* If $z=\pi_1\cdots\pi_t$ (primes) then $n=\prod N(\pi_i)$ and, by the classification, each $N(\pi_i)$ is $3$, a rational prime $p\equiv1\pmod3$, or $q^2$ with $q\equiv2\pmod3$. Hence every prime $q\equiv2\pmod3$ occurs in $n$ to an even power.

*Sufficiency.* If all $b_j$ are even, take $z=(-1+\omega)^k\prod\pi_j^{a_j}\prod q_j^{b_j/2}$ with $N(\pi_j)=p_j$; its norm is $3^k\prod p_j^{a_j}\prod q_j^{b_j}=n$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-2b.title: Count associate classes
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-2b.body:
**Lemma.** If $p\equiv1\pmod3$ and $p=\pi\bar\pi$ (with $\pi=a+b\omega$, $\bar\pi=a+b\omega^2$), then $\pi,\bar\pi$ are not associates. Suppose $\bar\pi=u\pi$. Then $\pi\mid\pi-\bar\pi=b(\omega-\omega^2)=b(2\omega+1)$ and $\pi\mid\pi+\bar\pi=2a-b$. Since $N(2\omega+1)=3\ne p$ and $\pi$ is prime, $\pi\nmid2\omega+1$, so $\pi\mid b$, hence $p=N(\pi)\mid b^2$ and $p\mid b$; similarly $\pi\mid2a-b$ gives $p\mid2a-b$, so $p\mid a$. Then $p^2\mid a^2-ab+b^2=p$, a contradiction.

*Counting.* Let $z$ have norm $n$. Every prime factor of $z$ has norm $3$ (an associate of $-1+\omega$), $p_j$ (an associate of $\pi_j$ or $\bar\pi_j$ by unique factorization of $p_j=\pi_j\bar\pi_j$), or $q_j^2$ (an associate of $q_j$). Comparing norms, $z$ is an associate of
$$(-1+\omega)^k\prod_j\pi_j^{c_j}\bar\pi_j^{\,a_j-c_j}\prod_jq_j^{b_j/2},\qquad0\le c_j\le a_j,$$
and by uniqueness of factorization (and the Lemma) different choices of $(c_j)$ give non-associate elements. There are $\prod(a_j+1)$ choices, and each class contains exactly $6$ elements (the unit multiples). Hence there are $6(a_1+1)\cdots(a_r+1)$ solutions $(a,b)$.

(Check: $2023=7\cdot17^2$ gives $6\cdot2=12$ solutions in integers, matching the $12$ elements found in Problem 4-1.) $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-3b.title: Congruences
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-3b.body:
If a prime $d$ divides $a$ and $b$, then $d^2\mid a^2+ab+b^2=c^2$, so $d\mid c$, contradicting $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$. So $\gcd(a,b)=1$.

Suppose $a\equiv b\pmod3$, say $b=a+3t$. Then $c^2=a^2+a(a+3t)+(a+3t)^2=3a^2+9at+9t^2\equiv0\pmod3$, so $3\mid c$ and $9\mid c^2$. Then $9\mid3a^2+9at+9t^2$ gives $9\mid3a^2$, so $3\mid a$ and $3\mid b$, contradicting $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$. Hence $a\not\equiv b\pmod3$, i.e. $a-b\equiv1$ or $2$, and in the latter case $b-a\equiv1\pmod3$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-3c.title: Factor $a-b\omega$ in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-4-3c.body:
Let $\alpha=a-b\omega$ and $\bar\alpha=a-b\omega^2$. Then $\alpha\bar\alpha=N(\alpha)=a^2+ab+b^2=c^2$.

*$3\nmid c$.* If $3\mid c$ then $a^2+ab+b^2\equiv0\pmod9$, and $(a-b)^2=a^2+ab+b^2-3ab\equiv-3ab\pmod 9$ gives $3\mid(a-b)^2$, so $3\mid a-b$, contradicting $a-b\equiv1\pmod3$.

*$\alpha,\bar\alpha$ have no common Eisenstein prime factor.* If $\pi$ divides both, it divides $\alpha-\bar\alpha=-b(\omega-\omega^2)=-b\omega(1-\omega)$. If $\pi\mid1-\omega$, then $\pi$ is an associate of the norm-$3$ prime $1-\omega$, so $3\mid N(\alpha)=c^2$, contradicting $3\nmid c$. Otherwise $\pi\mid b$ (as $\omega$ is a unit and $\pi$ is prime), then $\pi\mid\alpha+b\omega=a$; so $\pi$ divides both integers $a,b$ and hence (Bezout in $\mathbb Z$, $\gcd(a,b)=1$) divides $1$, impossible.

*Square structure.* For each Eisenstein prime $\pi\mid\alpha$ we have $\pi\nmid\bar\alpha$, so the exact power of $\pi$ in $\alpha\bar\alpha=c^2$ (which is even, as $c^2$ is a square of an integer) lies entirely in $\alpha$. Hence $\alpha=u\beta^2$ for a unit $u$ and some $\beta\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$; write $\beta=m-n\omega$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z$. Taking norms, $c^2=N(\beta)^2$ so $c=N(\beta)=m^2+mn+n^2$ (here $N(m-n\omega)=m^2+mn+n^2$). Since $c\not\equiv0\pmod3$ and $m^2+mn+n^2\equiv(m-n)^2\pmod3$, we get $m\not\equiv n\pmod3$.

*Removing the unit.* Every unit is a square of a unit ($\omega^j=(\omega^{2j})^2$), so absorb $u=\pm\omega^j$ into $\beta$: $\alpha=\pm\beta^2$ with $\beta=m-n\omega$ again of this form. Now $(m-n\omega)^2=m^2-2mn\omega+n^2\omega^2=(m^2-n^2)-(2mn+n^2)\omega$, so $a=\pm(m^2-n^2)$ and $b=\pm(2mn+n^2)$ (same sign). The minus sign would give $a-b=-(m^2-2mn-2n^2)\equiv-(m-n)^2\equiv-1\equiv2\pmod3$, contradicting $a-b\equiv1$. So $a=m^2-n^2$, $b=2mn+n^2=n(2m+n)$.

*Signs and coprimality.* Replacing $(m,n)$ by $(-m,-n)$ changes nothing in these formulas, so assume $n\ge0$. As $b>0$, $n\ne0$, so $n>0$ and $2m+n>0$. Since $a>0$, $|m|>n$; if $m<0$ then $m<-n$ and $2m+n<-n<0$, impossible. So $m>n>0$. Finally, a common divisor $d$ of $m,n$ gives $d^2\mid a,b,c$, so $d=1$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-1a.title: Two coordinate systems
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-1a.body:
*Existence of $a+b\omega$:* the degree-reduction of Problem 1-1 (via $\omega^2=-1-\omega$) works verbatim with rational coefficients.

*Uniqueness:* $1$ and $\omega$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb R$ (as $\omega\notin\mathbb R$), so if $a+b\omega=a'+b'\omega$ then $a=a'$, $b=b'$.

*Second form:* $\omega=-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i$, so $a+b\omega=\left(a-\frac b2\right)+\frac b2\,i\sqrt3$, with rational $c=a-\frac b2$, $d=\frac b2$. Conversely $c+di\sqrt3=(c+d)+2d\,\omega$ (check: $(c+d)+2d\left(-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i\right)=c+di\sqrt3$). Uniqueness follows because $1,i\sqrt3$ are independent over $\mathbb R$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-1b.title: Rationalise the denominator
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-1b.body:
Write $\alpha=a+b\omega$, $\beta=c+d\omega$ with rational $a,b,c,d$ (5-1a). Then $\beta\bar\beta=N(\beta)=c^2-cd+d^2\in\mathbb Q$ is positive ($\beta\ne0$), and $\bar\beta=c+d\omega^2=(c-d)-d\omega\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$. So
$$\frac\alpha\beta=\frac{\alpha\bar\beta}{N(\beta)}=\frac1{c^2-cd+d^2}\,(a+b\omega)\bigl((c-d)-d\omega\bigr)\in\mathbb Q(\omega),$$
because $\mathbb Q(\omega)$ is closed under products (as in 1-2) and under multiplication by rationals.

Conversely, take $z=\frac pq+\frac rs\omega\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$ with integers $p,q,r,s$ ($q,s\ne0$). Then $z=\frac{ps+qr\omega}{qs}$, a quotient of Eisenstein integers. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-2.title: Contradiction through $z^2$
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-2.body: Suppose $z\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$. Then $z^2=2-5+2i\sqrt{10}=-3+2i\sqrt{10}\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$, so $2i\sqrt{10}\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$ and dividing by $2i\sqrt3\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$ (5-1b) gives $\sqrt{10/3}\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$. This number is real, and in the form $c+di\sqrt3$ (unique) a real element has $d=0$, so $\sqrt{10/3}=c\in\mathbb Q$. But $\sqrt{10/3}=\frac{\sqrt{30}}3$ and $30$ is not a perfect square, so it is irrational. Contradiction. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-3.title: Two cases
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-3.body:
*Uniqueness (general).* If $f,g$ are two monic polynomials of the same minimal degree with root $\alpha$, then $f-g$ has smaller degree and root $\alpha$, so $f-g=0$.

*Existence.* If $\alpha\in\mathbb Q$, then $x-\alpha$ is monic of degree $1$, minimal (nonzero constants have no roots). Otherwise $\alpha=a+b\omega$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$, $b\ne0$, so $\alpha\notin\mathbb R$. Put
$$f(x)=(x-(a+b\omega))(x-(a+b\omega^2))=x^2-(2a-b)x+(a^2-ab+b^2)\in\mathbb Q[x],$$
(using $\omega+\omega^2=-1$ and $\omega\cdot\omega^2=1$). It has root $\alpha$. No linear rational polynomial vanishes at the non-real $\alpha$, so the minimal degree is $2$, and $m_\alpha=f$ by uniqueness. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-4.title: Gauss's lemma
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-4.body:
($\Leftarrow$) If $m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z[x]$ it is a monic integer polynomial with root $\alpha$.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be monic with $f(\alpha)=0$. Factor $f$ into monic irreducible polynomials in $\mathbb Z[x]$; $\alpha$ is a root of one of them, $g$. By Gauss's lemma $g$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[x]$. Divide in $\mathbb Q[x]$: $g=q\,m_\alpha+r$ with $\deg r<\deg m_\alpha$. Evaluating at $\alpha$ gives $r(\alpha)=0$, so $r=0$ by minimality, i.e. $m_\alpha\mid g$. Since $g$ is irreducible and monic, $g=m_\alpha$. Hence $m_\alpha=g\in\mathbb Z[x]$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-5.title: Both inclusions
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-5.body:
By 5-4, $\alpha$ is integral over $\mathbb Z$ iff $m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z[x]$.

*$\mathbb Z[\omega]\subseteq$ integral.* For an integer $a$, $m_a=x-a$. For $\alpha=a+b\omega$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Z$, $b\ne0$, $m_\alpha=x^2-(2a-b)x+(a^2-ab+b^2)\in\mathbb Z[x]$.

*Integral $\subseteq\mathbb Z[\omega]$.* If $\alpha\in\mathbb Q$ and $x-\alpha\in\mathbb Z[x]$ then $\alpha\in\mathbb Z$. Let $\alpha=a+b\omega$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$, $b\ne0$, and suppose $s=2a-b\in\mathbb Z$ and $N=a^2-ab+b^2\in\mathbb Z$. Then $4N=(2a-b)^2+3b^2=s^2+3b^2$, so $3b^2=4N-s^2\in\mathbb Z$. Write $b=\frac uv$ in lowest terms: $v^2\mid3u^2$ forces $v^2\mid3$, so $v=1$ and $b\in\mathbb Z$. Then $2a=s+b\in\mathbb Z$; write $a=\frac t2$. Now $N=\frac{t^2}4-\frac{tb}2+b^2\in\mathbb Z$ means $t^2-2tb+4b^2\equiv0\pmod4$, so $t(t-2b)\equiv0\pmod4$; if $t$ were odd, $t(t-2b)$ would be odd. So $t$ is even and $a\in\mathbb Z$. Thus $\alpha\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$. $\blacksquare$

chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-6.title: Conjugate polynomial trick
chmmc-cmm-2023-power-5-6.body:
Elements of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ are roots of $x-\alpha\in\mathbb Z[\omega][x]$, so they are integral over $\mathbb Z[\omega]$.

Conversely let $f(x)=x^n+\alpha_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+\alpha_0$ with $\alpha_j\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$ and $f(z)=0$. Let $g(x)=x^n+\bar\alpha_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+\bar\alpha_0$ (complex-conjugate coefficients). Since $\bar\omega=\omega^2\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$, $\bar\alpha_j\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$, so $fg\in\mathbb Z[\omega][x]$ is monic with $(fg)(z)=0$. The coefficient of $x^m$ in $fg$ is $c_m=\sum_{j}\alpha_j\bar\alpha_{m-j}$ (with $\alpha_n=1$, and $\alpha_j=0$ for $j>n$), and $\bar c_m=\sum\bar\alpha_j\alpha_{m-j}=c_m$, so $c_m$ is a real Eisenstein integer. A real element $a+b\omega$ has $b=0$, so $c_m\in\mathbb Z$. Thus $fg\in\mathbb Z[x]$ is monic with root $z$, i.e. $z$ is integral over $\mathbb Z$, hence $z\in\mathbb Z[\omega]$ by Problem 5-5. $\blacksquare$
